summary.value: The paper introduces ActiveCQ, a unified Bayesian framework for actively estimating a broad class of causal quantities (ATE, CATE, ATT, and ATE under distribution shift) from observational data. It reframes these quantities as integrals of an outcome regression function and models the regression with a Gaussian Process, pairing it with two alternatives for the distribution component: a conditional density estimator and, more centrally, conditional mean embeddings (CMEs) in an RKHS. The CME-based formulation yields closed-form GP posteriors for the target causal quantity, avoids explicit density estimation, and stays aligned with the GP’s feature space (Sec. 4.2–4.3; Prop. 1). Building on this posterior, the authors derive CQ-specific acquisition rules that directly reduce uncertainty of the estimator, instantiating information gain and total variance reduction with batch (greedy) selection (Sec. 4.5; Alg. 1). They provide convergence guarantees showing uncertainty decay rates under submodularity assumptions (Theorem 2; Sec. 4.6; App. E). Extensive simulations and semi-synthetic studies (IHDP, LaLonde) demonstrate consistent sample-efficiency gains over baselines across multiple CQs, especially under distribution shift (Fig. 2–5; App. F.6). The framework is modular and compatible with scalable GP approximations and alternative kernels (Remark 2; App. F.2, F.6.2).

strengths.value:
1. Clear, general problem formulation that goes beyond CATE. The paper crisply defines Active Estimation of Causal Quantities (ActiveCQ) and unifies ATE, CATE, ATT, and ATEDS via an integral representation (Lemma 1; Remark 1; Sec. 3). Including ATEDS (distribution shift) in the active estimation scope is particularly valuable for practice.

2. Technically elegant CME–GP unification yielding analytic posteriors for CQs. The use of Conditional Mean Embeddings with a GP regression gives closed-form mean/covariance of the CQ posterior (Proposition 1; Eq. 6), avoiding explicit conditional density estimation and Monte Carlo over s (Sec. 4.3). Operating in the same RKHS as the GP and updating the CME features after each round is a well-motivated, task-aligned design.

3. CQ-aware acquisition rules that target the estimator’s uncertainty directly. The IG and TVR criteria are instantiated for the CQ posterior (Eqs. 8–9; Sec. 4.5), with batch selection via a greedy scheme that promotes diversity (Eq. 10). The paper clearly explains their geometric differences through eigenvalue views (App. D.5, A- vs D-optimality), which is rare and insightful.

4. Theoretical uncertainty-decay guarantee tailored to the transductive, integral-estimation setting. Theorem 2 bounds the estimator variance by irreducible uncertainty plus a term scaling with γnB/√nB (Sec. 4.6), supported by a careful construction (Def. 2, Def. 5) and submodularity justification (App. E.1). Extending TAL-style analysis to distributional integrals is a meaningful theoretical contribution.

5. Strong empirical support across diverse CQs and settings. The method consistently improves sample efficiency in simulations and semi-synthetic data, most prominently under shift (DS) where gains are substantial (Fig. 2, DS panel; Fig. 5; Tables 1–2; App. F.6). Visualizations show that acquisitions align with the target distribution (Fig. 3), directly evidencing the intended behavior.

6. Thorough robustness and practicality analysis. The paper examines batch sizes, warm starts, pool sizes, kernels, and heteroscedasticity (Fig. 12–16; Fig. 11; App. F.6.2), and provides a running-time and complexity breakdown contrasting IG vs TVR (Fig. 4; App. F.5). This level of scrutiny is unusual and increases confidence in practical deployment.

7. Modular framework that clarifies where the gains come from. By providing both CDE/MDN and CME instantiations under a shared GP regressor, the paper isolates the value of the CME approach (Sec. 4.2–4.3; App. F.2–F.3). The analysis in App. G.2 convincingly argues why CME’s feature-aligned embeddings are advantageous in the active loop.

8. Careful derivations for multiple CQs and integral estimators. The appendices give step-by-step expansions for CATE, ATE, ATT, and ATEDS (App. D.1–D.4), all cast as standard GP predictions at “effective” inputs (feature tensors with mean/conditional embeddings). This unification improves clarity and reproducibility.

9. Precise positioning relative to neighboring fields. The distinctions from active causal discovery/ABCI and from transductive AL are carefully laid out (Sec. 6; App. B.2–B.3), making clear both the methodological and problem-setting differences and why previous methods are not baselines in this scenario.

10. Evaluation design that matches the learning objective. The paper explicitly defines the target set (Sec. 4.4) and justifies AMSE as the central metric rather than internal uncertainty (App. F.4.1), ensuring alignment between acquisition, estimation, and evaluation.

11. Reproducibility and implementation transparency. Detailed dataset generation, benchmarks, hyperparameters, and training protocols (App. F.1–F.3), plus an algorithmic overview (Alg. 1), support reuse and verification.

12. Elegant handling of distribution shift without density estimation. For ATEDS, the target population is incorporated via empirical mean embeddings (App. D.4; Eqs. 37–40), cleanly bridging source-trained regressors to new populations—a practically important and methodologically neat component.

weaknesses.value:
1. Theory hinges on strong, partly unverified assumptions; bounds are indirect and potentially loose.
   - The variance decay (Theorem 2; Sec. 4.6; App. E) relies on submodularity (Assumption 1). App. E.1 explicitly notes that for CATE and ATT “the assumption may not strictly hold,” and the proof appeals to weak submodularity via an Information Ratio. In addition, the analysis uses an Approximate Markov Boundary and constants depending on λmin(KXPXP) and γn (App. E.3–E.4), which can be ill-conditioned in practice. Finally, the proof bridges to γr defined over f, while “a formal connection” to the CQ-level γnB is left for future work (App. E.3, footnote).
   - Actionable: (i) Empirically verify (approximate) submodularity/diminishing-returns for IG/TVR on your settings; (ii) quantify constants (or provide kernel-dependent rates) for common kernels; (iii) tighten the analysis by directly bounding the CQ-level information gain (instead of via f), or provide an upper bound linking the two; (iv) add experiments showing empirical variance-vs-budget curves to assess the γnB/√nB trend.

2. Acquisition scalability remains a bottleneck; continuous treatments are curtailed by IG instability.
   - Despite the modularity claim (Remark 2), results and complexity still reflect O(nT^3) GP training and expensive greedy updates (Fig. 4; App. F.5). More critically, “IG-based methods may suffer from numerical instability when computing the determinant of large covariance matrices” (Sec. 5), and you avoid IG for continuous-treatment settings by discretization for tractability (App. F.6.3).
   - Actionable: (i) Implement sparse/inducing-point or SKI GPs and lazy/stochastic greedy (with incremental Cholesky) to show scalability; (ii) stabilize IG using logdet via Cholesky/LDLT with jitter, pivoted-Cholesky/Lanczos approximations, or Hutch++ trace-log estimators; (iii) approximate IG for continuous a via low-rank Nyström/Random Features on the CQ posterior and subsampled treatment grids; (iv) report wall-clock and accuracy on a larger pool (nP ≫ 10^3).

3. No uncertainty accounting for the learned CME; fully plug-in embeddings may miscalibrate CQ posteriors.
   - The method “obviates explicit density estimation,” but the CME itself is estimated from finite samples; uncertainty propagation is deferred to future work (Sec. 4.3; App. G.2). Without modeling this, the CQ posterior may be overconfident, especially under shift (ATEDS) or with sparse conditioning (ATT).
   - Actionable: Integrate uncertainty over the conditional operator (e.g., BayesIMP/IMPspec-style priors on operators), or provide a bootstrap/sandwich variance correction for CQ posteriors. Add ablations where CME sample size is varied to show its effect on calibration.

4. Evaluation leaves strong competitors underexplored for the transductive/shifted objective.
   - While baselines include µ-BALD, TVR, and QHTE (Sec. 5; App. F.2.3), transductive AL methods that reweight or select pool points to match a target distribution are discussed (App. B.2) but not instantiated. Given the paper’s core claim—align selection to P∗CQ—importance-weighted BALD/TVR or target-weighted coresets would be natural, stronger competitors.
   - Actionable: Add baselines that (i) reweight utilities by w(x) ∝ dP∗CQ/dPpool (estimated via density ratio or kernel mean matching) and (ii) incorporate target-aware diversity (e.g., target-weighted facility location/DPP). This will better isolate the benefit of your CQ-posterior-based acquisition vs. simpler, distribution-aware reweighting.

5. Mixed IHDP outcomes and validation mismatch undermine claims of broad robustness.
   - In the semi-synthetic IHDP, methods “do not consistently outperform random acquisition” for ATE/ATT (Fig. 23–24), and App. F.2.1 concedes the validation strategy is “not optimal” because it monitors performance on the observational distribution rather than the CQ target.
   - Actionable: Construct target-aware validation (e.g., via CQ-induced reweighting or CME-sampled validation) to select kernels/hyperparameters. Provide further diagnostics for cases where random wins (e.g., overlap/positivity, conditioning sparsity), and test multi-task kernels or S-/T-learners to share strength across treatment groups in these small-n, high-d settings.

6. Overlap/positivity and support gaps are not handled in the acquisition objective.
   - The framework assumes positivity (Sec. 2; App. C.1) but in observational pools, parts of (a, z, s) relevant for P∗CQ may have weak support. The current utilities can still prioritize such regions, but labeling cannot fix structural gaps, leading to extrapolation risk.
   - Actionable: Incorporate overlap-aware penalties or feasibility constraints into U(XB), e.g., downweight points whose effective leverage for P∗CQ relies on extrapolation (large posterior lengthscale distance or large importance weights). Report overlap diagnostics alongside performance.

7. ATT/CATE conditioning can be fragile under continuous treatments and imbalanced arms.
   - ATT relies on µs|ã (App. D.3), and CATE on µs|z (Sec. 4.3). With continuous a or sparse neighborhoods around ã or z, conditional operators estimated as Cs|a Caa−1 can be unstable; the paper circumvents this by discretizing treatments (App. F.6.3).
   - Actionable: Use conditional operator regression with robust regularization (e.g., Tikhonov with cross-validated λ; localized kernels), or nearest-neighbor CMEs for continuous conditioning; evaluate performance as P(a≈ã) varies.

8. Kernel alignment between GP and CME is mandated but only partially optimized.
   - Prop. 1 requires features ϕ(a), ϕ(z), ϕ(s) to “be updated after each batch” to match the GP’s product kernel (Sec. 4.3), yet the CME bandwidth is median-heuristic with a learnable λ (App. F.2.2). Kernel misalignment can bias the effective kernel k̄ and CQ posterior.
   - Actionable: Jointly learn CME and GP kernels by maximizing a CQ-marginal-likelihood (induced by Eqs. 6, 30–35), or employ deep kernels shared by both GP and CME; add ablations where GP–CME kernels are intentionally misaligned to demonstrate sensitivity/resilience.

9. Acquisition objectives are batch-greedy and can be expensive; diversity is ad hoc.
   - Batch selection uses greedy maximization of U(Xb) (Eq. 10), which triggers repeated posterior updates and high cost, and diversity is only implicitly enforced by the marginal-gain structure (Sec. 4.5; Fig. 4; App. F.5).
   - Actionable: Implement lazy/stochastic greedy, DPP priors for diversity, or submodular surrogates (e.g., facility location) weighted by CQ-relevance; compare against top-b for speed/quality trade-offs.

10. Empirical scope is limited to synthetic and semi-synthetic settings; cost heterogeneity is ignored.
   - While thorough (Fig. 2–5; App. F.6; Tables 1–2), there is no evaluation on large-scale observational data with heterogenous labeling costs, common in practice (Sec. 3 defines a uniform budget).
   - Actionable: Add a study with instance-dependent costs and demonstrate cost-aware acquisition (e.g., maximize U(XB)/cost(XB)); include at least one larger real observational dataset to evidence scalability and robustness beyond benchmarks.

11. Presentation artifacts impair reproducibility of derivations.
   - The appendices contain long sequences of LaTeX artifacts in equations (App. D.1–D.4), and stray symbols appear in the main text (e.g., “/hammer”, “/thumbtack” near Fig. 1). These obscure key matrix identities and kernel expressions needed to reimplement k̄ and cross-covariances.
   - Actionable: Clean the typesetting, provide a compact notation table for all effective kernels in Prop. 1 and Apps. D.2–D.4, and release minimal code snippets that compute ν(·) and q(·,·) for each CQ.

questions.value:
1. Submodularity and Theorem 2 applicability
   - Sec. 4.6 and App. E.1 note Assumption 1 may not strictly hold for CATE/ATT and appeal to weak submodularity via an Information Ratio. Can you empirically check diminishing-returns/submodularity (or report submodularity ratios) of IG/TVR on your settings, and quantify the constants (e.g., C1, C2) and the dependence on λmin(KXPXP)? This would help assess the tightness and practical relevance of Theorem 2’s bound (Eq. 12).

2. CQ-level information gain vs f-level γr
   - In App. E.3 you bound via γr defined over f and defer a formal link to the CQ-level γnB. Can you provide an upper bound that directly connects these two quantities (even if coarse), or a proposition bounding I(τ̂; yX) in terms of I(f; yX)? A sketch or lemma would materially strengthen the theoretical story.

3. Positivity/overlap enforcement during acquisition
   - App. E.1 says positivity is “maintained during acquisition.” How is this enforced in practice within UIG/UTVR (Eqs. 8–9)? Do you (a) downweight target regions with poor support, (b) reject acquisition points that would rely on extrapolation for τ̂, or (c) monitor overlap diagnostics? Please clarify, and consider adding an overlap-aware penalty or constraint to U(XB).

4. IG numerical stability and continuous treatments
   - Sec. 5 reports IG “may suffer from numerical instability” and App. F.6.3 discretizes treatments partly to avoid intractable determinants. What stabilizations did you try (e.g., Cholesky/LDLT with jitter, pivoted-Cholesky, Lanczos/trace-log approximations)? Could you include an experiment showing IG with stabilized logdet (or low-rank approximations) on a continuous-a setup, even if approximate, to quantify the gap vs TVR?

5. CME uncertainty propagation and calibration
   - Sec. 4.3 and App. G.2 highlight CME benefits but treat the embedding as plug-in. Can you (i) add a simple bootstrap over CME (or a BayesIMP/IMPspec-style operator prior) to propagate uncertainty into τ̂’s posterior, and (ii) report calibration (e.g., credible-interval coverage) for τ̂ under varying CME sample sizes? This would address potential overconfidence, especially for ATEDS/ATT.

6. Kernel alignment between GP and CME
   - Prop. 1 and Sec. 4.3 require updating ϕ(a), ϕ(z), ϕ(s) after each batch to “match the kernels learned in the GP,” while App. F.2.2 uses median-heuristic RBF for CME with a learnable λ. How closely aligned are the learned kernels in practice? Please add an ablation with deliberate GP–CME kernel misalignment to show sensitivity, or a joint optimization of CME/GP kernels (e.g., by maximizing a CQ marginal likelihood induced by Eqs. 6/30–35).

7. ATT/CATE conditioning stability with continuous variables
   - ATT relies on µs|ã and CATE on µs|z. App. F.6.3 notes treatment discretization; how stable is CME estimation when conditioning on a continuous a or rare z? Would localized/NN CMEs or stronger regularization (Tikhonov λ, localized kernels) help? A small experiment varying P(a≈ã) or the sparsity of z would be informative.

8. Transductive AL baselines under target shift
   - App. B.2 discusses TAL, but baselines (Sec. 5; App. F.2.3) do not include distribution-aware variants. Could you add (i) importance-weighted µ-BALD/TVR using a density-ratio/kmm-based w(x) ∝ dP∗CQ/dPpool, and (ii) target-weighted coresets or diversity (e.g., facility location/DPP with target weights)? This would better isolate the benefit of CQ-posterior-based acquisition vs. simpler target-aware reweighting.

9. IHDP diagnostics and target-aware validation
   - In IHDP ATE/ATT (Fig. 23–24) methods do not consistently beat random; App. F.2.1 notes validation mismatch. Can you provide: (a) target-aware validation (e.g., reweighted by P∗CQ or CME-sampled), (b) overlap/positivity diagnostics, and (c) a comparison with multi-task kernels or S-/T-learner GP variants to share strength across treatment arms? This may clarify whether the gap is due to model selection or fundamental data limits.

10. Batch selection scalability and diversity
   - Sec. 4.5 adopts greedy batch selection (Eq. 10); Fig. 4 shows cost increases with smaller batches. Can you implement lazy/stochastic greedy or incremental Cholesky/Woodbury updates to reduce cost and compare speed–quality trade-offs? A DPP or explicit diversity prior (beyond marginal-gain diversity) would also be a helpful baseline in Fig. 4.

11. Clarify ATEDS assumptions: which components shift?
   - Definition 1 (DS) and App. D.4 model τATEDS(a) integrating over ˜Ps, with samples ˜S (Eqs. 37–40). Does ˜P include shifts in treatment p(a) as well, or only covariates p(s)? Please clarify consistency with Assumption 6 (App. C.1) and specify requirements on available target data (covariates only vs. also treatments).

12. Sensitivity to target set specification (Sec. 4.4)
   - Results depend on the chosen (aI, ZI). How sensitive are acquisitions and AMSE to this choice (e.g., finer vs. coarser treatment grids, fixed z vs. random z)? A small sensitivity study would help practitioners pick target sets.

13. Empirical uncertainty–error relationship
   - Since acquisition optimizes τ̂’s posterior covariance (Eqs. 8–9), could you report the empirical relationship between marginal posterior variance and squared error of τ̂ (e.g., rank correlation) across rounds and methods? This would corroborate that uncertainty is a good proxy for error in your CQ setting.

14. Practical safeguards against extrapolation
   - Fig. 3 suggests the method aligns acquisitions to the target distribution. Do you also avoid selecting points whose leverage comes from long-range extrapolation in GP space (e.g., large kernel distances/importance weights)? A simple safeguard (e.g., cap on leverage scores or distance thresholds) and its effect would be useful to document.

15. Derivation clarity and minimal implementation recipe
   - App. D.1–D.4 contain rendering artifacts (“/dcurly…”), and Sec. 4.3/Prop. 1 compresses several kernel terms. Please provide a cleaned derivation and a minimal “effective-kernel” recipe (pseudocode) that computes k̄x,x′, k̄x,XT, KXT,XT for each CQ, plus a short code snippet for ν(·), q(·,·). This will materially aid reproducibility.

16. Larger-scale or cost-aware study
   - Fig. 4 and App. F.5 analyze runtime; could you include (i) one larger pool (nP ≫ 10^3) with a scalable GP (e.g., inducing points/SKI) to demonstrate modularity in practice, and (ii) a cost-aware acquisition variant (non-uniform label costs), which is common in observational studies? Even a synthetic cost model would be informative.
